pull.title: fuzz: torcontrol: drive the control connection over a mocked socket
pull.body:
The `torcontrol` fuzz target hands made-up replies straight to the `TorController` callbacks, and caps reply lines at 16 characters. As a result, most success paths can't be reached, and the code that parses the control port (`ProcessBuffer()`, `ReceiveAndProcess()`) never runs.

This rewrites the target around a fake Tor on the other end of a real `TorControlConnection`, connected through `DynSock`. Replies go over the wire. The fake Tor answers each command the controller sends with a reply of the matching shape, so inputs can complete the whole handshake: PROTOCOLINFO, authentication (including SAFECOOKIE), GETINFO and ADD_ONION. The harness also checks that reply data never splits a command or injects a new one.

The first commit fixes `DynSock::Wait()`, which deleted its own socket. The bug has been there since #30205; this target is the first caller.

### Testing

Line coverage of `src/torcontrol.cpp` goes from 52% on master to 81% after a 10-minute local run. The master number is from the qa-assets corpus. Most of what remains is the controller thread itself, which the harness replaces, and socket errors that `DynSock` can't produce.

The input format changes, so the corpus in qa-assets needs a refresh.

test: fix DynSock::Wait deleting its own socket

socket was deleted once that temporary went out of scope. Delegate to
Sock::Wait(), which wraps it without taking ownership.

comments.body: Thanks! I've applied the diff and removed the direct handler entirely since it's not needed anymore, because the fuzzer should be able to reach those state over the wire.

Thanks for the review! Makes sense for me, but `DynSock` inherits from `ZeroSock`, whose `Wait()` returns all requested events immediately, so removing the override would make `Wait()` resolve to `ZeroSock::Wait()` rather than `Sock::Wait()`. I've instead made `DynSock::Wait()` delegate directly to `Sock::Wait()`, which reuses its non-owning wrap.

Yes, that looks good,  sorry I missed the `ZeroSock`, thanks.

As a possible follow-up, a small unit test that `DynSock::Wait()` reports not-ready on an empty pipe and ready once data arrives.., would lock in both this fix and the `ZeroSock` distinction.

Nice! I've added the oracle to verify if the bitcoin node is sending the correct server hash, along others such as: each `SAFECOOKIE` client nonce is 32 bytes and never repeats. I've also added an assert that tor receives `-torpassword` exactly as configured, which catch the same issue being fixed by #36637.

I'll let the `-torpassword` oracle as a follow-up after this PR and that one get merged.

_non-blocking_ style nit: just wondering why a `struct` was chosen over a `class` here

generally, most readers will see a `struct` and expect a plain bundle of data, where each member can be touched on its own. this one has more going on: `Write()` keeps `pending` and `written_tail` consistent, and `NewConnection()` has to reset everything except `client_nonce`.

for this use case a `class` kind of looks like the more readable option. what do you think ?

i think it is safe to leave out the `COOKIE` authentication method. the controller never uses it (it only acts on `NULL`, `SAFECOOKIE` and `HASHEDPASSWORD`) so offering it does not reach any new code, and the Tor control spec [discourages](https://spec.torproject.org/control-spec/implementation-notes.html?highlight=__#:~:text=using%20the%20%22COOKIE,version%20of%20Tor.) it anyway
**nit**: `arg` is used in the `if (password.empty())`, it can be moved into that scope since that's where its only usage is

now that #36637 is merged, the only thing the `-torpassword` oracle is waiting on is this PR itself, and it is a change to this same file. could it go in here after a rebase ?

i do not see any harm in adding it here; it avoids a follow-up PR. but, if there is a reason to keep it separate (e.g. not wanting to restart review or keeping the diff smaller), that is fine, just curious what it is

I think is worth as a regression test. Let's say if a day bitcoin core makes a change and for some reason start parsing `COOKIE` messages. It's also a one line change that shouldn't decrease much the efficiency of the fuzz target.

The harness drives `FakeTor`'s state directly (pending, unanswered, pipes and others), so as a class everything would still be public. Hiding it would mean adding accessors to a test fake, which doesn't seem worth it. Stateful `structs` with methods are common in the fuzz tests, `SimTxGraph` for example, so I'll keep it as is.
